author: Claude (Gemini draft unavailable due to API quota; hand-authored to the same standard)
basis: New mission, no workbook source. Facts: 2016 DPP 'nuclear-free homeland' platform, written into the 2017 Electricity Act revision alongside the '20-30-50' 2025 generation-mix target; Maanshan Reactor 2 (Taiwan's last operating reactor) shut down 17 May 2025, ending nuclear power which had supplied ~4.2% of 2024 generation (288 TWh total, of which 42.4% gas / 39.3% coal / 11.6% renewables); 23 August 2025 referendum (Proposal No. 21) on restarting Maanshan: 74.2% yes among ~5.8M votes cast (~4.3M yes vs ~1.5M no) but failed procedurally because yes-votes fell short of the legal threshold of one quarter of registered voters (~5M of ~20M); Taiwan imports ~97% of its primary energy, with usable reserves estimated at about two weeks; Taipower accumulated losses of ~NT$418 billion, September 2025 rate rise ~3.12% (smaller than the 5-10% first proposed); 'energy trilemma' (security/equity/sustainability) framing per World Energy Council. Neutral on the nuclear debate throughout: trade-offs presented for all three options (restart, accelerate renewables, lean on gas), no side endorsed. Register per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md. Authored by Claude directly (Gemini 3.1 Pro was unavailable for this mission's draft pass due to an API quota limit reached mid-session; content was hand-written to the same standard and iteratively verified against scripts/quality.py and scripts/grammar_range.py).

slides.1: Just three months after formally switching off its final reactor, Taiwan asked the electorate whether nuclear power should resume. What shifted in that short interval is precisely what this discussion unpacks.
slides.2: SDG 7 calls for affordable, reliable and sustainable energy for everyone, although this talk narrows that lens onto nuclear power specifically. It uses the so-called energy trilemma, three aims that seldom align.
slides.3: Despite sounding recent, this policy is actually a decade in the making. A party voted into office in 2016 on a nuclear-free pledge saw that commitment codified into statute the following year.
slides.4: By 17 May 2025, the second reactor at Maanshan had been decommissioned permanently, closing the chapter entirely. Nuclear generation, once around 4 percent of 2024's total, vanished from the grid overnight.
slides.5: Since renewable capacity is still lagging behind its own build-out schedule, fossil-fuel plants have picked up nearly everything that nuclear power used to provide. More than 80 percent of 2024's electricity therefore came from coal and gas.
slides.6: Sentiment toward nuclear power has plainly reversed in recent months. Although 74.2 percent of votes cast favoured reviving Maanshan, overall turnout never actually reached the level Taiwan's law demands.
slides.7: Even while retiring nuclear capacity across a full decade, Taiwan has hardly been idle elsewhere. LNG terminals, offshore turbines and solar arrays have been expanded considerably across that same stretch.
slides.8: Both nuclear and renewable generation emit negligible carbon at the point of production, a trait fossil fuels simply lack. Displacing nuclear specifically with coal or gas therefore carries a measurable climate cost.
slides.9: Unlike weather-dependent sources, nuclear plants deliver steady output no matter the conditions outside, a trait engineers call baseload power. Solar and wind, by contrast, rise and fall constantly, which complicates balancing supply and demand.
slides.10: Had the referendum succeeded, reactivating the plant could have trimmed both emissions and cost fairly quickly. Doing so would nonetheless demand fresh safety audits and a degree of public confidence not yet secured.
slides.11: Pouring resources into renewables and storage instead carries real popularity and genuine public appeal. Nonetheless, that expansion already trails its own rollout plan, so it is no quick fix either.
slides.12: Turning further toward imported gas burns cleaner than coal and adapts more easily to changing electricity demand. Doing so, however, would deepen an import dependence that already leaves Taiwan strategically exposed.
slides.13: Taiwan's workable reserves stretch across roughly two weeks, while imports account for nearly 97 percent of total energy supply. Should a single shipment be delayed, that safety margin shrinks almost instantly.
slides.14: Taipower's cumulative losses have swollen to roughly NT$418 billion, a figure that keeps climbing. Continuing to fund new capacity without any change to sensitive prices will only deepen that hole.
slides.15: Climate commitments cannot be met without a substantial cut to the fossil share of generation. Neither a nuclear revival nor a faster rollout of renewables can arrive quickly enough to prevent continued reliance on gas.
slides.16: These three pressures constantly work against one another. Only when security, cost and emissions are jointly satisfied will any single pathway qualify as genuinely sustainable, and no option secures every goal for free.
slides.17: In summary, Taiwan retired nuclear power precisely as scheduled, only for voters to nearly reverse that outcome within months. The trilemma clarifies why no available option was ever going to be straightforward.
slides.18: This dilemma bears directly on those seated in this room. Engineers, rather than campaign slogans, will ultimately be the ones designing whichever reactors, grids or storage systems eventually resolve this tension.
slides.19: Let's commit to interrogating the emissions, cost and security figures first, before anything else. What genuinely matters is which problem a given technology solves, not which side feels more appealing to support.
slides.20: Let's close on a single guiding thought. Whichever comes next, a referendum or a grid blueprint, will be shaped by rigorous evidence or by persuasive slogans, and that outcome is now down to you.
